summary:
Nevada stands under the United States federal framework, which governs passports, entry screening, federal custody and federal care measures; those apply within the state and are carried by the national record. The findings below are those specific to Nevada.

A national legal risk assessment published in July 2026 places Nevada in its Low-Risk group, directly below the most-protective tier, crediting the state with fairly robust non-discrimination policies while finding it falls short on healthcare equity and on protections for incarcerated transgender people.

State anti-discrimination law covers gender identity or expression in employment, housing and public accommodations, effective 1 October 2011 and extended throughout the state statutes effective 1 July 2017. Protections covering sexual orientation alone came earlier: in public and private employment and in public accommodations from the 1999 legislative session, and in housing from the 2011 laws. In November 2022 voters approved Question 1 by 58%, adding sexual orientation and gender identity or expression to the state constitution's equal protection clause.

Hate-crime law provides additional penalties for offences motivated by listed actual or perceived characteristics; gender identity or expression was added by amendment effective 1 October 2013. A hate-crime reporting hotline was established in January 2025. The gay panic defence was repealed by legislation signed 14 May 2019, effective 1 October 2019, and the state's 1983 HIV-specific offences were repealed by SB 275, signed in May 2021 and effective immediately, following a 2019 law creating an HIV task force.

State identity documents are comparatively open. Since 2016 the state vital records office has issued a birth certificate with a corrected gender on two affidavits, with no requirement for sex reassignment surgery, and driver's licences and state IDs can be changed on the same basis. An X third-gender designation is available on driver's licences, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation, introduced in 2019. Legislation passed in May 2017 and signed on 22 June 2017 abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before obtaining a legal sex change on government documents. These rules govern Nevada documents; federal travel documents follow the rules set out in the national record.

On public bathrooms and facilities, Nevada's position is assessed against the Movement Advancement Project's Equality Map, which tracks state-by-state rules on whether transgender people may use public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity.

Marriage and partner recognition: a federal appellate court struck down the state's constitutional ban on same-sex marriage on 8 October 2014 in Sevcik v. Sandoval. The marriage statute has used gender-neutral language since 1 July 2017, and in November 2020 voters removed the constitutional ban with 62% support. In December 2020 the Nevada Supreme Court required retroactive recognition of out-of-state same-sex marriages performed before 2014. The Nevada Domestic Partnership Act, effective 1 October 2009 after a veto override, grants many of the rights of marriage but exempts private and public employers from providing medical coverage to domestic partners, leaves parental rights less well defined and carries uncertain recognition outside the state.
tangentialFactors:
Nevada's Low-Risk placement in the July 2026 assessment puts it in the group below the most-protective tier alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia: protective on non-discrimination, weaker on care access and on people in custody.

The X designation Nevada offers applies to state-issued licences, birth certificates and IDs only. A traveller whose document set also includes federal travel documents needs the national record for the marker rules that apply to those.

Coverage has advanced in Nevada through narrower instruments than the omnibus approach. The governor vetoed the broader SB 302 package in 2023, and a coverage mandate was vetoed on 22 June 2017 before the state Medicaid agency acted in March 2018; the narrower insurer-coverage bill passed in June 2023 became law.

School sports eligibility changed through an association rule rather than a statute: the state athletics association reversed its own 2016 policy in April 2025, while a governor-supported 2026 ballot initiative to set eligibility generally by sex assigned at birth failed to reach the November 2026 ballot.
localsOnly:
Health insurance and care access: state law bars health insurers from discriminating against transgender patients. In March 2018 the state Medicaid agency announced it would cover sex reassignment surgery, after a coverage mandate was vetoed on 22 June 2017. A bill passed in June 2023 and signed by the governor requires health insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments, effective 1 January 2024; the broader SB 302 omnibus, which would have shielded gender-affirming care and abortion, was vetoed.

Correctional facilities: legislation approved in May 2023 explicitly protects transgender and intersex people in the state's correctional facilities. The July 2026 assessment's finding that Nevada falls short on protections for incarcerated transgender people does not itemise which practices produce it.

Schools: SB 504, effective 1 July 2015, names gender identity or expression as a protected ground in the anti-bullying law and directs school policies on reporting, parent notification and staff training. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires high-school transgender athletes to compete according to sex assigned at birth. A governor-supported 2026 ballot initiative to determine school sports eligibility by sex assigned at birth failed to reach the November 2026 ballot.

Conversion therapy on minors is banned under a bill signed 17 May 2017, effective 1 January 2018.

Family formation: same-sex relationships have not been a legal barrier to adoption; state law since 2017 reflects equal parental rights; lesbian couples may access in vitro fertilisation with recognition of the non-genetic, non-gestational mother regardless of marital status; gestational surrogacy is permitted and recognised equally, while traditional surrogacy contracts are illegal.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Equality Map's specific classification of Nevada within its tally of bathroom and facilities rules is not recorded in the material reviewed, so the state's precise position on that comparison is unresolved.

The July 2026 assessment does not state which healthcare-equity measures or which incarcerated-population practices led to its two adverse findings, or whether the May 2023 correctional-facilities law was taken into account.

The status of any successor legislation to the vetoed SB 302 omnibus after the June 2023 insurer-coverage bill is not sourced here.

Federal measures, including passport markers, entry screening, federal custody policy and federal care rules, apply inside Nevada but are documented in the national record rather than in this state-level assessment.
